questions.prompt: A cross-origin API GET reaches the server, but its response lacks the needed CORS permission. What can happen in a browser fetch?

choices.text: The server cannot have received any request unless CORS permission was already present.
The browser exposes the body but strips only the disallowed response headers.
The browser can deny script access even though the server processed the request.
The response is readable because a GET request never needs CORS response checks.

questions.explanation: CORS governs browser response access. Some requests are sent without a preflight, so a server can process a request whose response script cannot read.

questions.prompt: A cross-origin fetch sends a custom `X-Trace-ID` header. What normally happens before the actual request?

choices.text: The header is safelisted because its name starts with the conventional X- prefix.
The browser sends a preflight to check permission for the non-safelisted header.
GET always avoids preflight regardless of its custom headers.
Only a non-safelisted method can trigger preflight, not a non-safelisted header.

questions.explanation: Non-safelisted request headers can trigger a CORS preflight even for GET. The method alone does not guarantee a preflight-free request.

questions.prompt: A cross-origin fetch uses `credentials: include`. Which allow-origin response value is compatible with credentialed CORS access?

choices.text: The requesting origin explicitly, with the required allow-credentials permission.
A wildcard origin with allow-credentials true is enough for include mode.
A wildcard origin is enough because include bypasses response origin checks.
An allowed request cookie is enough even if allow-credentials is missing.

questions.explanation: Credentialed CORS requires an explicit matching origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. A wildcard origin is not sufficient in that mode.

questions.prompt: fetch receives an HTTP 404 response with no network or CORS failure. What should application code normally inspect?

choices.text: The rejected fetch promise, because every non-2xx status rejects it.
Only Content-Type, because HTTP error statuses are hidden from every Response.
The absence of a Response, because 404 always becomes a fetch network error.
The fulfilled Response status or ok value before processing the error body.

questions.explanation: HTTP error status does not itself reject fetch. The application checks Response.status or ok; network and CORS errors are different failures.

questions.prompt: A developer sets `mode: no-cors` hoping to read an unrestricted cross-origin JSON body. What response is exposed in that mode?

choices.text: A normal readable response whose custom headers alone are hidden.
A normal readable response as long as the server response is valid JSON.
An opaque response whose body and status are not exposed normally.
A readable response if the request used GET and did not include credentials.

questions.explanation: No-cors is not a way to bypass CORS for readable data. Cross-origin responses in that mode are opaque to script.

questions.prompt: A browser prepares a CORS preflight for a non-safelisted request method. What is the preflight HTTP method?

choices.text: HEAD checks response availability but does not send the intended request method.
OPTIONS asks the server about the proposed cross-origin request.
The actual method runs first, followed by an OPTIONS response-permission check.
GET checks permission whenever the actual request has no body.

questions.explanation: A CORS preflight uses OPTIONS with fields describing the intended request. It is separate from the actual operation.

questions.prompt: A team reviews its CORS assumptions. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: CORS permission controls cross-origin response exposure.
Some cross-origin requests can be sent before a response access check.
no-cors exposes arbitrary cross-origin JSON to script.
CORS is not server authentication for arbitrary clients.
A missing allow-origin always proves the server never saw the request.

questions.explanation: a: The browser checks whether script may receive the response. b: Safelisted requests need not preflight. c: Its cross-origin response is opaque. d: Non-browser clients are not governed by browser CORS enforcement. e: The server may have processed a non-preflighted request.

questions.prompt: A review asks when CORS preflight is needed. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A non-safelisted method can trigger preflight.
A preflight sends the application request body to test whether it is valid.
Every GET avoids preflight regardless of its headers.
Every POST Content-Type is automatically safelisted.
A non-safelisted custom header can trigger preflight.

questions.explanation: a: Methods outside the safelist require permission checking. b: Preflight checks permission using OPTIONS, not the actual application operation body. c: Non-safelisted headers can still require it. d: Only specified media types and constraints meet the safelist. e: Header names and values participate in the preflight decision.

questions.prompt: A cross-origin API uses cookie credentials. Which CORS claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The response needs allow-credentials true for that access.
A wildcard allow-origin grants credentialed access by itself.
include disables all origin checks for the response.
include requests credential inclusion subject to other cookie rules.
Credentialed access needs an explicit matching allow-origin.

questions.explanation: a: The credentialed CORS check requires it. b: That combination fails the credentialed check. c: CORS checking still applies. d: Credentials mode participates in whether credentials are sent. e: A wildcard does not satisfy include mode.

questions.prompt: An application handles fetch results. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A network failure always returns a readable 500 Response.
Opaque responses expose a normal readable cross-origin body.
HTTP 500 alone does not require fetch rejection.
Response.ok can distinguish successful status codes.
A consumed response body can always be read a second time without a prior clone.

questions.explanation: a: A network error rejects rather than synthesizing that HTTP response. b: Opaque filtering hides body and status details. c: An HTTP error can still yield a Response. d: It represents the 200 through 299 range. e: A disturbed body cannot simply be consumed again; clone before consuming when multiple reads are needed.
